new_statements.quote: Kayan languages also have penultimate stress, but actively shift stress to the final syllable if the penult is a schwa (Clayre and Cubit 1974 for Baram River Kayan; Smith 2017a for Data Dian Kayan, spoken in Indonesia). [...] [p. 26:] In the dialect of Kayan spoken in Data Dian gemination is observed after a penultimate schwa but not after other vowels (Smith 2017a). As noted earlier in §3.2.2, Kayan usually has penultimate stress, but, in examples with a schwa in the penult, stress is word-final. [...] (19) Data Dian Kayan (Smith 2018b) təpaʔ [təpːáʔ] 'pound rice' səpun [səpːún] 'great grandparent', mətaŋ [mətːáŋ] 'ask' dənaʔ [dənːáʔ] 'slow'

As noted earlier in §3.2.2, Kayan usually has penultimate stress, but, in examples with a schwa in the penult, stress is word-final.' followed by ex. (19) 'Data Dian Kayan (Smith 2018b) təpaʔ [təpːáʔ].. səp…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Kayan River Kayan as recorded at Data Dian (Apo Kayan), word stress is regularly penultimate; when the penultimate syllable has a schwa nucleus, stress shifts to the final syllable and the onset consonant after the schwa is geminated (Malay-type schwa-conditioned penult/final pattern). Stress is non-contrastive. Note that for citation/list forms Kayan varieties are elsewhere reported with final stress (Blust 1977 Uma Juman: final in citation forms, penultimate in phrases; Cubit 1964 Baram Kayan: usually final on disyllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the schwa condition (open penult with ə -> final stress with gemination); p. [10] adds the general Austronesian remark that list or citation intonation often places stress on the final syllable even in penultimate-stress languages, 'see Blust 1977 for examples from Kayan'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, stated as the usual (conversational) pattern; the article contrasts this with citation/list intonation, which in Kayan can be final (Blust 1977). The statement rests on Smith's own 2015-16 Data Dian fieldwork (cited as Smith 2017a/2018b), but the dissertation itself prints no stress sentence for Kayan, so this article is the only place the observation is published.
new_statements.identity_note: waha1239/whu is a Glottolog Bookkeeping (spurious) languoid. Ethnologue 16-28 classify 'Kayan, Wahau' under Kayan Proper, 500 speakers (Wurm & Hattori 1981), north of Muara Wahau on a north tributary of the Telen; Revel-Macdonald 1982 ('Ky' = Kayan Uma' Lakan, Miau Baru, Wahau River), Guerreiro 1996:222 (Kayan U. Lekan/U. Lasan on the Wahau-Telen-Merah rivers) and ethnographic snippets (BRB 1984; Objets et Mondes 1978; Sellato 2012) identify this as the Kayan Uma' Lekan community that moved from Long Heban / Apo Kayan (Kayan River) to Miau Baru in 1969-83, i.e. a diaspora of Kayan River Kayan [xkn] kaya1325, Glottolog dialect umal1240 'Uma Lakan'. The quoted statement describes Kayan River Kayan as spoken at Data Dian (Apo Kayan, North Kalimantan; Smith's consultant Kornelius), not the Miau Baru settlement and not necessarily the Uma' Lekan dialect; it should be filed under kaya1325 (whose an earlier compilation classification was no source found) rather than as a separate language. Under Glottolog's alternative reading (whu = Wehea Modang, moda1244/liah1237) the applicable statement would instead be Smith 2017:73 / Smith 2019 'strong word-final stress' (see).

readall_conflicts: The one work opened (Cubit 1964, Baram Kayan, Sarawak) gives non-phonemic stress 'usually on last syllable' (2-syllable words) / 'usually on third syllable' (3-syllable words) with no vowel or weight condition, whereas the existing statement for the language's source variety (Smith 2022 Diachronica pp. [14], [26], Kayan River Kayan of Data Dian, Apo Kayan) gives penultimate stress that shifts to the final syllable only when the penult holds a schwa. Smith 2022 also attributes the same schwa-conditioned penultimate pattern to Baram River Kayan citing Clayre & Cubit 1974, which is not what Cubit 1964 states for Baram Kayan; the likeliest reconciliation is Blust 1977's citation-form-final versus phrase-medial-penultimate observation for Kayan, and Cubit's examples are all isolated citation forms, but Cubit himself does not say so. The two sources describe different Kayan varieties (Baram Kayan bara1370 vs Kayan River Kayan kaya1325), so this is a cross-variety disagreement rather than a contradiction about waha1239 itself, for which no source says anything about stress.
